name: Computer Networks - Performance & Metrics
description: Bandwidth, throughput, delay components (propagation, transmission, processing, queuing), jitter, utilization, and performance calculations (CCN02)

questions.question: A household runs 3 simultaneous streams, each needing 8 Mbps. Adding 25% extra headroom for overhead and bursts, what minimum Internet rate should you target?
questions.explanation: Three streams × 8 Mbps = 24 Mbps base. Adding 25% overhead: 24 × 1.25 = 30 Mbps. Always add headroom above the raw requirement to account for protocol overhead and traffic bursts.

questions.question: A lab has 92 wired PCs. You use 24-port switches, but must reserve 2 ports per switch for uplinks/expansion. How many switches are required?
questions.explanation: Each switch has 24 − 2 = 22 usable host ports. 92 ÷ 22 = 4.18, which rounds up to 5 switches. Always ceiling-divide when computing equipment counts since partial switches must be whole units.

questions.question: A link rate is 80 Mbps. Ignoring overhead, approximately how many megabytes per second (MB/s) is this?
questions.explanation: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 80 Mbps ÷ 8 = 10 MB/s. This bit-to-byte conversion is fundamental: network speeds are quoted in bits per second while file sizes are in bytes.

questions.question: A protocol stack has 5 layers. Processing at each layer adds 0.6 ms per packet in one direction. Ignoring transmission time, what is the one-way processing delay per packet?
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 layers contributes 0.6 ms of processing delay: 5 × 0.6 = 3.0 ms total. Processing delay accumulates at each layer as headers are added/removed and the packet is examined.

questions.question: A sales team has 80 employees. Each downloads 30 records/day and each record is 5 KB. How much data is downloaded per day (ignore protocol overhead)?
questions.explanation: 80 employees × 30 records × 5 KB = 12,000 KB = 12 MB per day. This type of capacity planning calculation determines how much bandwidth and storage a business application requires.

questions.question: A Wi-Fi LAN has a raw rate of 54 Mbps. One-third of capacity is lost to overhead/contention, and the remaining capacity is shared equally by 9 active users. About how much throughput does each user get?
questions.explanation: 54 Mbps × (2/3) = 36 Mbps effective capacity after overhead. Divided among 9 users: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 Mbps per user. Wireless overhead from CSMA/CA, headers, and contention typically consumes one-third or more of raw capacity.

questions.question: An application sends 1000 bytes of data. Encapsulation adds 20 bytes (transport) + 20 bytes (network) + 18 bytes (link). What is the total size on the wire?
questions.explanation: 1000 + 20 + 20 + 18 = 1058 bytes. Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) during encapsulation, increasing the total size transmitted on the physical medium.

questions.question: In SI units, what does the prefix 'k' (kilo) represent?
questions.explanation: In SI (metric) units, kilo (k) means 10³ = 1,000. Note the difference from binary kibibyte (KiB = 2¹⁰ = 1,024); in networking, SI prefixes are used for data rates (kbps, Mbps, Gbps).

questions.question: A link has a bandwidth of 80 Mbps and is utilized at 75% during a transfer. What is the achieved throughput?
questions.explanation: Throughput = Bandwidth × Utilization = 80 × 0.75 = 60 Mbps. Utilization captures the fraction of link capacity actually carrying useful data; overhead, idle time, and collisions reduce utilization below 100%.

questions.question: A network service has 99.99% availability. Approximately how much downtime does this allow per year?
questions.explanation: 99.99% availability means 0.01% downtime. In a year (≈525,600 minutes): 0.0001 × 525,600 ≈ 52.6 minutes. The 'four nines' standard is a common SLA target for enterprise services.

questions.question: A packet experiences: Processing 3 ms, Queuing 7 ms, Transmission 4 ms, Propagation 16 ms. What is the total end-to-end delay?
questions.explanation: Total delay = 3 + 7 + 4 + 16 = 30 ms. The four components of packet delay are processing (inspection), queuing (waiting in buffer), transmission (putting bits on wire), and propagation (travel time across medium).

questions.question: A router can process 2,000 packets/s. Traffic arrives at 1,600 packets/s. What is the utilization (rho)?
questions.explanation: Utilization ρ = arrival rate / service rate = 1,600 / 2,000 = 0.8. As ρ approaches 1.0, queuing delays grow dramatically — this is a key insight from queuing theory applied to network design.

questions.question: A signal travels 3,000 km over optical fiber where propagation speed is 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is the propagation delay?
questions.explanation: Propagation delay = distance / speed = 3,000,000 m / (2 × 10⁸ m/s) = 0.015 s = 15 ms. Propagation delay depends only on distance and medium; it is independent of link bandwidth or packet size.

questions.question: Four packets experience one-way delays of 30 ms, 35 ms, 50 ms, and 45 ms. What is the maximum jitter (max minus min delay)?
questions.explanation: Jitter = max delay − min delay = 50 − 30 = 20 ms. Jitter measures variation in packet arrival times; high jitter disrupts real-time applications like voice and video that expect regular packet arrival.

questions.question: How long does it take to transmit a 12 MB file over a 24 Mbps link, ignoring propagation and queuing delays?
questions.explanation: 12 MB = 12 × 8 = 96 Mb. Transmission time = 96 Mb / 24 Mbps = 4 seconds. Transmission delay is the time to push all bits of a packet/file onto the link, determined by size and link rate.

questions.question: Which utilization level is most likely to cause exploding queuing delay?
questions.explanation: At very high utilizations (near 100%), queuing delay grows toward infinity per queuing theory. At 98% utilization, even small traffic bursts cause queues to build up faster than they can drain.

questions.question: What does jitter refer to in the context of network performance?
questions.explanation: Jitter is the variance or inconsistency in packet delivery delay. Even if average delay is acceptable, high jitter means some packets arrive much later than others, which breaks real-time audio and video synchronization.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of jitter in packet networks?
options: Non-uniform processing delay at each hop
questions.explanation: Queuing delay is highly variable because it depends on traffic load at a given instant, which fluctuates as other flows compete for the same queue. Propagation and transmission delays are deterministic and do not cause jitter.

questions.question: Which type of application is most sensitive to jitter?
questions.explanation: Real-time voice and video streams must deliver data at a constant rate to reconstruct audio/video smoothly. Jitter disrupts this timing, causing garbled audio or choppy video. Elastic applications like email and file transfer are jitter-insensitive.

questions.question: Which technique is commonly used to reduce the effect of jitter at the receiver?
questions.explanation: A playback buffer (jitter buffer) absorbs variation by holding incoming packets briefly before playing them out at a smooth, constant rate. It trades a small increase in latency for consistent playback.

questions.question: When a link operates near capacity, which component of delay grows fastest?
questions.explanation: Queuing delay is the only delay component that is load-dependent; it grows non-linearly (approaching infinity as utilization → 100%). The other three components are fixed for a given link and packet size.

questions.question: A 1,200-byte packet is sent over a 16 Mbps link. Ignoring all other delays, what is the transmission delay?
questions.explanation: 1,200 bytes × 8 = 9,600 bits. Transmission delay = 9,600 / (16 × 10⁶) = 0.0006 s = 0.6 ms. Transmission delay is proportional to packet size and inversely proportional to link bandwidth.

questions.question: A 50 Mbps link carries 20 Mbps of traffic. What is the link utilization?
questions.explanation: Utilization = actual traffic / capacity = 20 / 50 = 0.4 = 40%. Low utilization means the link is lightly loaded with minimal queuing delay, while high utilization risks congestion.

questions.question: A 100 Mbps link with 20% protocol overhead. What is the effective net throughput?
questions.explanation: Net throughput = 100 × (1 − 0.20) = 80 Mbps. Protocol overhead (headers, ACKs, retransmissions) consumes a fraction of raw bandwidth, reducing the effective data rate available for application payload.

questions.question: 3 routers each add 0.9 ms of processing delay. 4 links each add 0.6 ms of transmission delay. What is the total delay?
questions.explanation: Processing: 3 × 0.9 = 2.7 ms. Transmission: 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 ms. Total = 2.7 + 2.4 = 5.1 ms. Multi-hop paths accumulate per-hop delays; routers add processing delay while links add transmission delay.

questions.question: A 40 Mbps Ethernet link is productive 60% of the time. What is the effective throughput?
questions.explanation: Effective throughput = 40 × 0.60 = 24 Mbps. Only 60% of link time carries actual payload; the rest is consumed by idle periods, headers, and protocol overhead.

questions.question: A signal travels 400 km over fiber at 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is the propagation delay?
questions.explanation: 400 km = 400,000 m. Propagation delay = 400,000 / (2 × 10⁸) = 0.002 s = 2.0 ms. Light travels at roughly 2/3 the speed of light in fiber, giving approximately 5 μs per km of propagation delay.

questions.question: A 50 Mbps link consumes 100 W. What is the energy per bit transmitted?
questions.explanation: Energy per bit = power / bit rate = 100 W / (50 × 10⁶ bits/s) = 2 × 10⁻⁹ J/bit = 2 nJ/bit. Energy efficiency is an increasingly important metric for network equipment design.

questions.question: A buffer holds 10 packets; 15 packets arrive simultaneously. How many packets are dropped?
questions.explanation: The buffer can hold 10 packets; 5 packets exceed capacity and are dropped (tail-drop). Buffer overflow and packet loss occur when arrival rate temporarily exceeds service rate and available buffer space.

questions.question: A 300 km fiber link at 2 x 10^8 m/s has a propagation delay of:
questions.explanation: 300,000 m / (2 × 10⁸ m/s) = 0.0015 s = 1.5 ms. This is a standard propagation delay calculation: convert km to m, divide by propagation speed.

questions.question: A home network supports 3 simultaneous video streams each requiring 10 Mbps. Adding 25% overhead headroom, what minimum Internet speed should be selected?
questions.explanation: Base requirement: 3 × 10 = 30 Mbps. With 25% headroom: 30 × 1.25 = 37.5 Mbps. Internet plans should always exceed the raw application requirement to handle protocol overhead and bursts.

questions.question: A packet traverses 4 routers each adding 0.8 ms, and 5 links each adding 0.5 ms transmission delay. Propagation is negligible. What is the total delay?
questions.explanation: Processing: 4 × 0.8 = 3.2 ms. Transmission: 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 ms. Total = 5.7 ms. On a multi-hop path, both per-router processing and per-link transmission delays accumulate.
